details:
What It Does & How It Works

Project AMDS is an explainable astronaut health-monitoring and decision-support platform built for long-duration spaceflight across the International Space Station, the Moon, and Mars. Rather than presenting passive vital-sign charts or black-box AI diagnoses, AMDS guides crew members and flight surgeons through a closed-loop workflow: Collect, Assess, Explain, Act, and Reassess.

The platform organizes astronaut wellbeing into nine NASA-grounded domains—Cardiovascular, Sleep & Circadian, Behavioral & Psychological, Musculoskeletal & Physical Fitness, Immune & Microbiological, Radiation Monitoring, Environmental & Life Support (ECLSS), Sensorimotor & Neurological, and Nutrition—alongside separate event-based Operational Risk Records (such as EVA hypoxia or decompression concerns) and Mission Context parameters. Using each astronaut's personal historical baseline, a deterministic intelligence engine detects statistical baseline drift, uncovers cross-domain patterns (such as sustained sleep reduction co-occurring with elevated resting heart rate and cognitive fatigue), recommends structured next steps, and evaluates whether indicators improve, remain unchanged, or worsen after countermeasures are logged.

Benefits & Intended Impact

As missions travel farther from Earth, communication delays and limited medical resupply reduce access to real-time ground support. AMDS adapts consultation guidance to mission one-way light time—distinguishing live ISS telemedicine from autonomous onboard workflows and asynchronous store-and-forward downlink packets on Mars transit missions—helping crews spot multi-system health changes early while keeping medical decisions transparent and scientifically grounded.

What Makes It Creative & Key Design Factors Considered

- Medical Safety & Epistemic Honesty: Instead of inventing unverified clinical thresholds, AMDS explicitly distinguishes validated standards from personal statistical baseline drift (Z-score deviation) and never diagnoses conditions or calculates individual radiation cancer probabilities.

- Data Provenance & Quality Integrity: Every measurement carries explicit provenance (ACTUAL_TELEM, MANUAL_ENTRY, SIMULATED), modality (wearable sensor, lab assay, subjective self-report, cabin sensor), and quality status (VALID, SUSPECT, MISSING). Missing or overdue lab panels trigger an INSUFFICIENT_DATA state rather than defaulting to "Normal," and suspect sensor spikes are flagged on charts without corrupting personal baselines.

- Habitat vs. Physiology Separation: Spacecraft cabin telemetry (such as cabin CO2 or pressure) is explicitly separated from personal physiological measurements so environmental anomalies are never confused with clinical vitals.

- Interactive Judge Simulation Engine: Includes four deterministic, clock-anchored simulated mission scenarios (Nominal ISS Baseline, Mars Transit Circadian & Autonomic Drift, Closed-Loop Post-Action Recovery, and EVA Operational Incident with ECLSS Drift) so users can test multi-domain alerts and reassessment loops end-to-end.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

- Backend & Intelligence Engine: Python 3.14, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy 2.0, SQLite, Pytest, Uvicorn, and uv.

- Frontend & Visualization: React, TypeScript, and Recharts (rendering broken line segments for missing telemetry and isolated warning markers for suspect sensor readings).

- Collaboration & Testing: Git/GitHub with automated Pytest contract, statistical drift, and reassessment test suites.

- Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure: Large language models and AI coding assistants (Gemini and Antigravity) were used during development to brainstorm system architecture, refine API contracts, generate boilerplate backend/frontend code and unit tests, draft documentation, and create synthetic demonstration telemetry scenarios. The runtime health-assessment engine itself is strictly deterministic and does not rely on an LLM to evaluate astronaut health.
